title: Blind hearts
hookLine: it is not the eyes that go blind but the hearts in the chests (22:46)

lines: A TOWER WITH NO ONE INSIDE.
cards: A caravan route in Arabia runs past ruins: a well nobody draws from, a tall, strong building with no one inside. Travelers pass them on the way north to Syria, water the camels nearby, maybe glance up.
They've seen them a hundred times. They're scenery.
Surah Al-Hajj points at exactly this kind of place, a town fallen in on its own roofs, a deserted well, a lofty tower, and then asks the travelers a question about their own eyes.

teach.b: Verse forty-six begins with a question: haven't they traveled in the land, so that they might have hearts to understand with, and ears to hear with? Then the line this day is named for.

teach.h: NOT THE EYES THAT GO BLIND.
teach.b: Pickthall: "For indeed it is not the eyes that grow blind, but it is the hearts, which are within the bosoms, that grow blind." Their eyes worked perfectly. They saw the ruins.
What didn't happen was understanding. The verse puts seeing somewhere other than the eyes: hearts to understand with.
In the Qur'an, the heart, qalb, is where a person understands, decides and takes things in, not only where they feel.
Some scholars connect the word with a root about turning; in that picture, the heart is the part of you that can turn.
A hadith in Bukhari says there is a piece of flesh in the body: if it's sound, the whole body is sound, and if it's corrupt, the whole body is corrupt, and that piece is the heart.
Notice the odd little phrase, the hearts within the bosoms. Everyone knows where hearts are.
Commentators suggest the extra words are there for force: this is the real heart meant, the one inside you, not a figure of speech. So the verse isn't scolding anyone for poor eyesight.
It describes an ordinary kind of blindness, the kind that comes from familiarity. The ruin you pass daily. The person you've stopped really looking at.
The sky you haven't checked in weeks.

how: Muslim teachers often quote 22:46 when speaking about reflection, and the Qur'an's repeated call to travel and consider the ruins of past peoples is part of how many Muslims think about history.

o: seeing with the eyes but not understanding
a loss of eyesight sent as a punishment
a heart too broken by grief to love again

games.q: inside the verse — tap the pairs.

s: in the Qur'an, the heart is mainly the seat of feelings
22:46 speaks of hearts to understand with: the qalb is where a person understands and decides.

games.q: you've passed the same ruined town on every caravan trip for years. what does the surah want you to do with it?
o: avoid that route; ruins are bad luck.
stop seeing scenery, and let it make you understand.
nothing; ruins are just old buildings.
games.why: travel so that you have hearts to understand with. the eyes had already seen it; the heart hadn't.

practice: Pick one thing in front of you that you see every day, a mug, your hand, the view from the window, and look at it as if you'd just arrived from very far away. Where did it come from, who made it, what has it been through?
Let your eyes rest there until the understanding catches up; if you pray, you can ask for a seeing heart.

wordCard.voice: Blind hearts. In Surah Al-Hajj, it isn't the eyes that go blind, but the hearts within the chests: seeing without understanding. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: the hearts; singular qalb; some scholars connect it with a root about turning.
